desc: EG&G is the company that made the secret sites work. Founded by MIT's Harold Edgerton with Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier, it instrumented and fired US nuclear tests from the Manhattan Project onward and became the classified services contractor for the Nevada complex - the Nevada Test Site and the Air Force operating location near Groom Lake. Its Special Projects organisation ran the unmarked passenger flights from McCarran to the Nevada ranges. Its role is documented not by acknowledgment but by litigation and by presidential fiat: workers who alleged exposure to burned hazardous waste at the Groom Lake facility sued in the 1990s, and rather than defend the facts, the government invoked the state secrets privilege and every President from 1995 forward signed an annual determination exempting the unnamed Air Force operating location near Groom Lake from environmental disclosure requirements. The Ninth Circuit upheld dismissal in Kasza v. Browner, 133 F.3d 1159 (1998), and the Supreme Court denied certiorari. That is the clearance infrastructure in its purest form: a facility whose environmental compliance is exempted by the President each year because acknowledging what is in it would harm national security. The custody allegation attaches through Alfred O'Donnell, the first general manager of EG&G in Nevada, who told George Knapp that a recovered saucer and a live being existed - and through Bob Lazar's 1989 claim, reported by Knapp, that he was employed at S-4 via EG&G. Richard D'Amato is reported to have named EG&G alongside Lockheed and Northrop as a feasible corporate home for the cover-up.

claims.text: EG&G was founded in 1947 by MIT figures Harold "Doc" Edgerton, Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier and became a principal contractor to the Atomic Energy Commission at the Nevada Test Site.

EG&G's Las Vegas-based Special Projects division provided engineering, technical, radar and logistical support for classified programs at Groom Lake and operated the passenger terminal at McCarran International Airport used for the unmarked Janet shuttle service to Groom Lake and the Tonopah Test Range.
A Nevada Department of Transportation diagram for McCarran International Airport dated May 1999 labels the Janet operations building the "EG&G Airlift Terminal."

Scheduled Las Vegas-to-Groom Lake flights date to 1972, initially flown with a Douglas DC-6; current operations are reported at over 20 weekday round trips carrying between roughly 1,000 and 1,500 workers to Groom Lake and Tonopah.

In August 1994 Professor Jonathan Turley of George Washington University's National Law Center filed Frost v. Perry (D. Nev. CV-S-94-714-PMP) against the Secretary of Defense and Kasza v. Browner (D. Nev. CV-S-94-795-PMP) against the EPA Administrator, RCRA citizen suits by former workers at the classified operating location near Groom Lake, based on field research by the Project on Government Oversight.

Six plaintiffs were permitted to proceed under pseudonyms on the ground that "there is a substantial danger here that the Plaintiffs will be subject to retaliation by the government or possible physical attack and harassment from third parties in Nevada"; the CIA, which "maintains a presence at nearby Area 58," was not named as a defendant.

Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall invoked a formal claim of military and state secrets privilege over categories of national security information associated with the operating location near Groom Lake, "specifically including '[s]ecurity sensitive environmental data,'" supported by unclassified and classified declarations; the district court also reviewed in camera a classified declaration by Air Force Vice Chief of Staff General Thomas S. Moorman, Jr.

The Air Force obtained summary judgment on the ground that the privilege barred presentation of any evidence tending to confirm or disprove that hazardous waste had been generated, stored or disposed of at the operating location — an essential element of every claim — notwithstanding the district court's finding that the plaintiff's need for discovery was compelling.

Presidential Determination No. 95-45 of September 29, 1995, 60 Fed. Reg. 52823, states: "I find that it is in the paramount interest of the United States to exempt the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada (the subject of litigation in Kasza v. Browner (D. Nev. CV-S-94-795-PMP) and Frost v. Perry (D. Nev. CV-S-94-714-PMP)) from any applicable requirement for the disclosure to unauthorized persons of classified information concerning that operating location."

Presidential Determination No. 95-45 exempts the location, pursuant to 42 U.S.C. 6961(a), "from any Federal, State, interstate or local provision respecting control and abatement of solid waste or hazardous waste disposal that would require the disclosure of classified information concerning that operating location to any unauthorized person," and states "This exemption shall be effective for the full one-year statutory period" — meaning the exemption must be reissued annually to remain in force.
The Ninth Circuit decided the consolidated appeals on January 8, 1998: Kasza v. Browner, 133 F.3d 1159 (9th Cir.), cert. denied, 525 U.S. 967 (1998), before Judges Wood, Rymer and Tashima.

The Ninth Circuit held that "if seemingly innocuous information is part of a classified mosaic, the state secrets privilege may be invoked to bar its disclosure and the court cannot order the government to disentangle this information from other classified information," and further that "we discern no Congressional intent to replace the government's evidentiary privilege to withhold sensitive information in litigation by providing an exemption from RCRA's regulation of hazardous waste. Accordingly, we hold that RCRA § 6001 does not preempt the state secrets privilege."

EG&G, Inc.'s Technical Services Division was acquired on August 20, 1999 by ETS Acquisition Corp., a subsidiary of Carlyle-EG&G Holdings Corporation; URS Corporation acquired all of the capital stock of the resulting company on August 22, 2002.
URS was acquired by AECOM in 2014, and the Janet operation is reported to be performed for the U.S. Air Force by Amentum, which acquired AECOM's federal and defense services business.

Kasza v. Browner is one of the most cited modern state secrets precedents and appears in Department of Justice briefing in later privilege cases, making the Groom Lake litigation the doctrinal ancestor of subsequent dismissals.
dossier.denialPosture: Neither EG&G nor its successors has ever publicly described the Groom Lake work. The government's posture in the Frost and Kasza litigation was not denial but non-cognizability: it did not deny that hazardous waste had been burned, it asserted that the existence or non-existence of such information is a state secret. Presidential Determination 95-45 preserves that posture explicitly, stating that nothing in it is intended to "imply that in the absence of such a Presidential exemption, the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) or any other provision of law permits or requires disclosure of classified information to unauthorized persons."
dossier.narrative:
Harold "Doc" Edgerton, Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier came out of MIT and out of the Manhattan Project's photographic and timing instrumentation work, and in 1947 incorporated the company that carried their initials. EG&G's core business for decades was the measurement of nuclear detonations for the Atomic Energy Commission — high-speed photography, timing and firing, diagnostics — making it one of very few private firms holding continuous clearances into the most sensitive American technical programs. From that base it grew into site services, security support, range operations and personnel logistics across the Nevada complex.

The most visible artifact is the airline. EG&G Special Projects operated the passenger service, universally known by its Janet callsigns, that moves the workforce from Las Vegas to the Air Force operating location at Groom Lake and to the Tonopah Test Range. A Nevada Department of Transportation diagram for McCarran dated May 1999 labels the building on the west side of the field the "EG&G Airlift Terminal." Reporting places the first Las Vegas-to-Groom flights in 1972 with a Douglas DC-6, and current operations at roughly twenty round trips per weekday carrying one to one and a half thousand workers on unmarked aircraft. This is what a routinized, industrial-scale commute to an unacknowledged facility looks like, and it has looked like that for over fifty years.

The legal history is the part that matters most for this board. In August 1994, Professor Jonathan Turley of the National Law Center at George Washington University filed two suits based on field research by the Project on Government Oversight: Frost v. Perry against the Secretary of Defense and Kasza v. Browner against the EPA Administrator, both in the District of Nevada, both under the citizen-suit provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Helen Frost was the widow of a former worker at the site; Walter Kasza was another. Six plaintiffs were permitted to proceed under pseudonyms because, in the district court's finding, "there is a substantial danger here that the Plaintiffs will be subject to retaliation by the government or possible physical attack and harassment from third parties in Nevada."

The government's response was not to deny the allegations. Once discovery began, the Air Force refused to furnish almost all requested information on privilege grounds, and Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall invoked a formal claim of military and state secrets privilege over categories of national security information associated with the operating location near Groom Lake, "specifically including '[s]ecurity sensitive environmental data.'" The claim was supported by an unclassified declaration and a classified declaration reviewed in camera, and the court also reviewed in camera a classified declaration by Air Force Vice Chief of Staff General Thomas S. Moorman, Jr. The district court found the privilege properly invoked and held that it covered the requested information "even though her need for discovery was compelling." The Air Force then moved for summary judgment on the ground that the privilege barred any evidence tending to confirm or disprove that hazardous waste had ever been generated, stored or disposed of at the location — an essential element of every claim. Summary judgment was granted.

On the EPA side, the district court held that RCRA itself contains no exception for disclosure of classified information, but that the President may exempt a federal facility under 42 U.S.C. 6961(a), and gave the Administrator time to obtain one. On 29 September 1995 the President issued Presidential Determination No. 95-45, published at 60 Federal Register 52823, which reads in operative part: "I find that it is in the paramount interest of the United States to exempt the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada (the subject of litigation in Kasza v. Browner (D. Nev. CV-S-94-795-PMP) and Frost v. Perry (D. Nev. CV-S-94-714-PMP)) from any applicable requirement for the disclosure to unauthorized persons of classified information concerning that operating location." It exempted the location from "any Federal, State, interstate or local provision respecting control and abatement of solid waste or hazardous waste disposal that would require the disclosure of classified information concerning that operating location to any unauthorized person," and stated: "This exemption shall be effective for the full one-year statutory period." One year. It must be renewed, and it has been.

The Ninth Circuit decided the consolidated appeals on 8 January 1998. Kasza v. Browner, 133 F.3d 1159, cert. denied, 525 U.S. 967 (1998). The panel held that the state secrets privilege is absolute; that "if seemingly innocuous information is part of a classified mosaic, the state secrets privilege may be invoked to bar its disclosure and the court cannot order the government to disentangle this information from other classified information"; and that RCRA section 6001 does not preempt the privilege — "we discern no Congressional intent to replace the government's evidentiary privilege to withhold sensitive information in litigation by providing an exemption from RCRA's regulation of hazardous waste." The Supreme Court declined review.

What that sequence establishes is not that anything exotic was buried in the Groom Lake trenches. It establishes that a contractor-operated installation the government declines to name can be placed outside an ordinary environmental statute by a one-page presidential memorandum; that a cabinet secretary's declaration can foreclose discovery of the physical facts; that federal courts will accept a mosaic theory under which even innocuous data is protected; and that the workers who get sick have no remedy. Every element a concealed recovery and exploitation effort would need to survive litigation was demonstrated in public between 1994 and 1998.

The corporate lineage matters for tracking who holds the contracts today. EG&G's technical services business was acquired in August 1999 by a Carlyle Group entity and operated as EG&G Technical Services; URS Corporation acquired it in August 2002; URS was absorbed by AECOM in 2014; and the Janet operation is reported to have passed with AECOM's federal business to Amentum. The initials survive on the fuselages of nothing, but the function has never been interrupted.
openQuestions: Whether the Presidential Determination has been reissued in every year since 1995 and under which presidents; the determination is expressly one-year and a complete Federal Register series has not been assembled here.
Which corporate entity currently holds the Groom Lake support and airlift contracts, under what contract number, and at what value — none of which appears in FPDS or any public award database.

Whether EG&G or its successors have ever held a waived DoD special access program contract, which would be recorded on a classified DD Form 254 provided to the cognizant security office under DoDI 5205.11 and not otherwise disclosed.
What the classified Widnall and Moorman declarations actually say about activities at the location; they remain sealed.
Whether Robert Lazar's claim of an EG&G-mediated hiring process for work at S-4 in 1988-89 can be corroborated by any employment, payroll or badge record; no such record has been produced.
Whether any of the missing or deceased individuals tracked on this board were EG&G, URS, AECOM or Amentum employees, and whether their assignments touched the Nevada complex.
dossier.whatItIs: EG&G — Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier — was founded in 1947 by three MIT-connected figures whose wartime work instrumented and photographed nuclear detonations, and became the Atomic Energy Commission's principal test-instrumentation contractor at the Nevada Test Site. Its Las Vegas-based Special Projects division provided engineering, technical, radar and logistical support to classified programs at the Air Force operating location near Groom Lake and operated the unmarked passenger airline known as Janet from a dedicated terminal at McCarran International Airport. The name and the contracts have since passed through the Carlyle Group, URS Corporation, AECOM and Amentum.
dossier.whyImplicated: EG&G is the connective tissue of the American black-site system: the same firm that instrumented nuclear tests ran the workforce airlift, the technical support and the site services that make an unacknowledged installation function. Its employees are the population at the center of the only litigation that has ever forced a court to decide what legal protection a denied facility enjoys. When Groom Lake workers sued in August 1994 alleging illegal open-air burning of hazardous waste, the Secretary of the Air Force filed a formal military and state secrets privilege claim covering categories that expressly included "security sensitive environmental data"; the President signed an annual RCRA exemption for "the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada"; and the Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that seemingly innocuous information forming part of a classified mosaic may be withheld and that a court cannot order the government to disentangle it. That sequence — contractor workforce, denied facility, state secrets, presidential exemption, dismissal — is the complete legal template a legacy program would require, and it is fully documented in the Federal Register and the Federal Reporter.
